I remember the beginning of my travels most clearly through the journal I kept—a battered notebook that became the only proof, some nights, that I had been anywhere at all. In its pages I recorded the names of cities and streets, the hour I arrived somewhere and the hour I fled, the small collisions between myself and the world that passed for experience. Some entries ran for pages, breathless accounts of light falling a certain way across a canal or the particular sound a language makes when you don't understand a word of it. Others documented the moments I could not write about directly: the times emotion rose up too fast and toppled me, when I sat on curbs or church steps with my head in my hands, unable to do anything but let it pass through me like weather.

The journal was not always so generous with language. There were days when all I could manage was a single mark—an "x" scratched into the margin, a small confession that something had happened here, something I could not yet name, something I trusted my future self to return to and decode. I imagined that later, with distance, the "x" would bloom back into meaning, that I would remember what it stood for the way you remember a smell before you remember the room it belonged to. Sometimes I was right. Often I was not, and the "x" remained just that, a private hieroglyph pointing at nothing but its own mystery.

Now, so much later, I find myself in a different kind of stillness. I am sitting near the Winter Palace with a beer sweating in my hand, the summer light doing something generous and unhurried to the façade in front of me, gilding it the way memory gilds everything eventually. There is no urgency in this moment, only the small physical pleasure of cold beer against warm air, and I let myself have it without apology, without reaching for the notebook.

Earlier, inside, I had stood before a set of stained-glass windows depicting the martyrdom of Stephen—his body given over to the stones, his face rendered in that particular medieval calm that suggests suffering transfigured rather than merely endured. Around him, the glass onlookers watched with the fixed, patient expressions of figures meant to teach: this is what mercy costs, this is what witnessing demands. Real onlookers stood before the glass ones, tourists and pilgrims alike, absorbing some fraction of the lesson whether they meant to or not.

To get there at all, I had needed help of a different kind. The plaza outside the Palace is vast, paved in pale limestone that seems to throw the sun back twice as hard, and I could not have crossed it—could not have summoned the will to walk that distance, to stand in line, to hand over the entrance fee and pass through the doors—without the amphetamines dissolving quietly in my system, lending me a borrowed, brittle energy. It is not a proud confession, but it is an honest one: some days the difference between staying outside and going in is chemical, is a small pill doing the work that willpower alone no longer can.

# Journal Fragments: A European Passage

The train pulls out of Limoges at dawn, and already I am reaching for the notebook—that battered companion whose pages have become the only fixed point in a journey defined by motion. The porcelain city recedes into fog and memory simultaneously, and I write: *7:14 AM, departure, grey light, a woman across the aisle weeping without sound.* This is how it begins, how it always begins—the compulsion to fix what cannot be held, to pin the butterfly of experience before it dissolves into the general blur of travel.

By the time Marseille appears—that assault of light and salt and shouting—the journal has become something else entirely. No longer simple record but a kind of scaffolding, an architecture I am building beneath my own dissolving sense of self. *The harbor smells of diesel and old fish. A man sells lottery tickets with three fingers missing from his left hand. I cannot remember what I ate yesterday.* The gaps between entries grow more telling than the entries themselves—what falls away, what refuses documentation, becomes its own kind of testimony.

There are afternoons when the pen simply stops. When the weight of continuous movement—city after city, station after station, the endless negotiation of unfamiliar currencies and unfamiliar tongues—produces not inspiration but a kind of paralysis. I sit in cafés and watch the world happen without me, unable to translate sensation into language, unable to perform the small violence of selection that writing requires. These are the moments of near-collapse, when the journey threatens to become simply accumulation without meaning, motion without narrative.

It is amphetamines that rescue the narrative, if rescue is the word—that chemical clarity that arrives like false dawn, sharpening the edges of perception until the world seems suddenly available again, suddenly capturable. Under their influence, Marseille sharpens into specific streets, specific faces, the specific weight of Mediterranean light at 4 PM. But this is not simply pharmaceutical propulsion—there is will beneath it, a stubborn insistence that the journey must continue, must be documented, must eventually arrive somewhere.

And arrival means the Winter Palace, that improbable destination glimpsed first in guidebooks and now approaching through the accumulated fatigue of weeks on trains, in stations, in the peculiar half-life of the perpetual traveler. The gates themselves become symbolic before I even reach them—not simply architecture but threshold, the promise that this scattered accumulation of moments might cohere into something like a completed journey, a finished self.

The final entries grow terse, almost telegraphic: *Cold. Legs ache. The gates are gold in this light.* As if language itself is depleting alongside the body, as if the closer one comes to arrival, the less need there is for elaborate documentation. The journal has done its work—has held together, however imperfectly, the fragments of a self scattered across geography and time.

What remains, finally, is the gate itself—vast, indifferent, magnificent—and the narrator standing before it, propelled by chemical will and stubborn persistence, having transformed mere movement through space into something resembling narrative, resembling meaning. The journal closes not with resolution but with threshold: the sense that documentation and travel alike are perpetual acts of becoming, that the self is not discovered but continuously constructed, entry by entry, station by station, until the moment arrives—cold, exhausted, illuminated—when one simply steps through.

# The Unlikely Threads Between Two Towns

There is something quietly fascinating about the way history weaves connections between places that, on the surface, seem to have nothing in common. Limoges, the elegant French city renowned for its porcelain and enamel work, and Altenkirchen, a modest town nestled in Germany's Westerwald region, are separated by hundreds of kilometers, a national border, and centuries of distinct cultural development. Yet there are threads—thin, but real—that tie such places together in the broader tapestry of European history.

Limoges rose to prominence in the Middle Ages, first as a center of exquisite enamel craftsmanship and later, from the 18th century onward, as the heart of French porcelain production. The discovery of kaolin clay deposits nearby transformed the city into a byword for fine ceramics, its name becoming synonymous with quality tableware exported across the globe. The city also carries a darker historical weight: it was near Limoges, in the village of Oradour-sur-Glane, that one of the most infamous atrocities of the Second World War took place in 1944.

Altenkirchen, by contrast, has a quieter historical profile. Its name—meaning "old church"—hints at its medieval origins, and it has long served as a regional administrative center in the Rhineland-Palatinate. Like countless small German towns, it experienced the upheavals of religious conflict, industrialization, and the wars that reshaped the continent.

There is, perhaps, no dramatic shared narrative binding Limoges and Altenkirchen directly. Instead, what connects them is something more universal: the way European towns and cities, regardless of size or fame, carry within them layers of craft, conflict, faith, and resilience. Both places remind us that history is not only made in capitals and battlefields, but in the accumulated life of ordinary towns—each with its own quiet claim to memory.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a free-verse poem about traveling alone in Europe, mixing memories of journaling with surreal, dreamlike imagery.
counterfactuals.output:
**Notebook with a Loose Spine**

I filled three notebooks that spring, ink bleeding
through pages like rain through a coat sleeve,
and somewhere between Lisbon and a dream
I stopped knowing which entries were real.

*Day 9: The pigeons in the square
speak Portuguese better than I do.
Bought bread. Cried a little. Fine.*

At night the hostels became boats,
their bunk beds rocking gently on a sea
that wasn't there, and I'd wake at 3 a.m.
convinced the ceiling was a sky
I hadn't paid for yet.

In Prague, a woman on the tram
had my grandmother's hands—
the same rings, the same soft weather
in her knuckles—and when I looked again
she was gone, replaced by a window
full of spires bending like wet grass.

*Day 14: Found a church with no doors.
Or maybe I imagined the doors were gone.
Wrote a postcard to no one. Sent it anyway.*

The trains blurred countries into watercolor—
France dissolving into Belgium
dissolving into a field of sunflowers
that turned, all at once, to face me
like a congregation mid-sermon.

I kept a list of things I saw twice:
the same red umbrella in three different cities,
a busker playing the same four notes
in a language of pure longing,
my own reflection, always slightly older
than I remembered leaving home.

*Day 21: Slept in a room shaped like a question mark.
The window opened onto yesterday.
I did not go through it. I wanted to.*

Somewhere in Vienna, or maybe in the space
between Vienna and a memory of Vienna,
I met a version of myself
sitting alone at a café,
writing in a language I hadn't learned yet—
and she looked up, unsurprised,
as if she'd been expecting
the arrival of her own ghost.

*Final entry, unnumbered:
I don't know which days were real
and which were the fever of being
so completely unwitnessed.
Maybe that's what alone means—
becoming your own unreliable narrator,
your own soft evidence,
the only witness to a life
that kept slipping, gently,
into something like a dream
you're still not sure you've woken from.*

I came home with empty notebooks
and a suitcase full of ticket stubs,
each one a small anchor
to a city that may or may not
have been waiting for me at all.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a poem that blends travel nostalgia, drug use, and religious iconography like stained-glass windows depicting saints.
counterfactuals.output:
# Pilgrim's Confession

The train ticket in my pocket
still smells of Lisbon rain,
folded soft as a rosary bead
worn thin from too much praying.

I lit up somewhere outside Porto,
watched the smoke curl toward heaven
like incense in that cathedral
where Saint Anthony's stained-glass eyes
followed me down the nave,
all amber and cobalt judgment,
his painted hands forever
reaching for something
I'd already lost.

The pills in Barcelona tasted
like communion wafers—
dissolved on the tongue
with the same solemn promise
of transcendence, of light
breaking through glass
in fractured, holy colors.

I confess: I found God
in the wrong places,
in hostel bathrooms and
midnight train compartments,
in the particular blue
of a Madonna's robe
rendered in glass a thousand years ago,
in the way morphine hums
like a choir
when you're far from home
and every church bell
sounds like it's ringing
just for you.

Saint Sebastian, arrows and all,
watched me from a chapel wall in Rome
while something chemical
bloomed golden in my chest—
both of us pierced through,
both of us performing
our own kind of ecstasy
for an audience of dust and pigment.

I carry these cities in my veins now,
these saints, these substances,
these windows that scatter light
like something sacred
even when I know
I'm the one who's broken it.

*Forgive me, Father,
for I have traveled,
and I have not repented,
and the stained glass
still glows
like it's waiting
for me to come home.*
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a literary poem referencing Limoges, Altenkirchen, and the Winter Palace, exploring themes of memory, illness, and pilgrimage.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Cartography of Forgetting

In Limoges the enamelists once fired
blue into copper, patient as a fever
that will not break—each vessel kiln-desired,
each glaze a small eternity in amber.
I think of this when memory runs thin,
when what I loved becomes a colored surface,
brilliant, hard, and hollow at its rim—
a saint's face rendered in a dead man's purpose.

At Altenkirchen, where the old church stands
alone against the Baltic's grey erosion,
the pilgrims come with maps drawn by their hands,
not knowing what they seek beyond devotion.
The steeple leans the way a body leans
when it has carried something far too long—
not toward collapse, but toward whatever means
the difference between silence and a song.

I was ill that winter, if you want the truth,
the kind of illness that rearranges rooms
inside the skull, rebuilds the halls of youth
with doors that open onto other tombs.
I dreamed the Winter Palace, its parade
of malachite and gilt, the Neva freezing
under windows where the light delayed
its own arrival, endlessly appeasing

some emperor of absence. In the dream
I walked those floors the way the ill will wander—
half-search, half-surrender to the theme
of finding what was never lost, but yonder,
always yonder, in another room.
The palace guards were paintings of the guards.
The guards were paintings of a guarded tomb.
I woke still holding all my broken shards—

Limoges blue, the Baltic church's lean,
the frozen river no one could persuade
to keep its distance from the in-between
of memory and marrow, thought and blade.
We travel to the places we have lost
already, in the mind's cathedral, dim
with candles no pilgrimage has crossed
except the one that carries us to Him

or nothing—call it what you will, the shrine
is always half-imagined, half-decayed,
like fever dreams of palaces, the fine
enamel work of grief that will not fade.
I am the pilgrim now. I am the glaze.
I am Altenkirchen's stubborn lean.
I am the Neva frozen in its ways,
uncertain what its stillness even means.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an experimental narrative poem about a traveler's journal entries, amphetamine use, and a vision of a saint in a basilica, ending at the gates of a grand palace.
counterfactuals.output:
**JOURNAL OF THE WHITE ROAD**
*(entries kept by an unnamed traveler, transcribed as found)*

---

**Day One — border town, no name given**

Woke before the birds, which means
I did not sleep. Chalked a line
of confidence onto my tongue
and swallowed the whole gray morning
in one clean gesture.

*The road is a throat and I am what it swallows.*

Legend says: this pass leads to a palace
white as a molar, gated in gold.
I have three coins, two feet,
and a heart that has started
keeping its own time —

tap tap tap-tap tap
tap tap-tap-tap-tap

— faster than the church bells,
faster than the crows leaving the wires.

---

**Day Two (or still Day One, unclear)**

No sleep. No hunger either. I ate
the idea of an apple and it sufficed.
The pill count in my pocket
goes down like a confession —
five, four, four, three —
I keep recounting. The number
keeps lying to me.

*Everything sharp. Everything named twice.*

Grass: green-green.
Sky: blue-blue-blue.
My hands: a stranger's, doing
excellent, tireless work
of simply shaking.

---

**Day Four — somewhere with a river, or the memory of one**

I have started talking to the milestones.
They do not answer but they lean,
attentive, the way old men lean
at fences to watch a fight.

Wrote in the margin: *I am almost there.*
Wrote below it: *there is not a place.*
Both true. Both mine.

The jaw aches from a grinding
I don't remember starting.
The teeth are keeping a beat
the ears can't hear.

---

**Day Six — the basilica, unplanned**

Ducked inside for shade, for silence,
for the cool stone hush that swallows heat
like a held breath.

And she was there.

Not a statue — I checked, I touched
the plaster foot, cold, ordinary —
but standing *beside* it, the same saint
doubled, haloed in the exact frequency
of my pulse, gold going
tap tap tap-tap tap
around her head like flies made of light.

She said (or the church organ said it,
or my blood said it through my ears):

*You have been walking toward a door
that was never closed.*

I wept. I am not embarrassed
to write that I wept, kneeling
on stone worn soft by four hundred years
of other people's knees,
other people's need
to be told the road forgives them.

She did not touch me.
She only stood there being made of light
and old wood and my own
unslept, overclocked devotion,
and when I looked again
she was only paint, only gesso,
only a woman someone carved
in 1490 to bear a hunger
she never asked to carry.

I stayed until the shaking slowed
to something almost like a heartbeat
instead of a machine's.

---

**Day Seven — no more counting pockets**

Threw the last two into the river
that may or may not exist.
Watched them go white, then gone,
small pills like teeth
the road had finally
knocked loose.

---

**Day Eight — the gates**

And here they are: gold,
exactly as promised, exactly
as overstated — gates
tall as the hunger that carried me,
a palace behind them
white as a tooth, as a saint's throat,
as the nothing
I have been racing toward
since the first sleepless morning.

I put my hand on the bars.
They are only metal.
Cold the way the plaster foot was cold.
Real the way the ache in my jaw is real.

I do not know if they will open.

I only know I got here
on my own legs, in my own skin,
carrying a small and human fire
I lit myself and could not, in the end,
put out —

and that the gate,
unopened,
is still a kind of arrival.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
